turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Look at most watches, and you will see the hour hand moving slowly around the dial. But some watches show the hour in a very different way. They have a small window with a number in it. At the end of each hour, the number does not change slowly. It jumps. One moment you see a ten, and the next moment you see an eleven. This is called a jumping hour.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The idea is old. Watchmakers made jumping hour pocket watches more than one hundred years ago. It looks a little like a digital display, but there is no battery and no screen. Everything is done with gears and springs.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So how does the number jump? Inside the watch, a small spring slowly stores energy during the hour. Think of pulling back a bow before you shoot an arrow. When the minute hand reaches twelve, a lever lets go, and the spring releases its energy all at once. The hour disc snaps forward to the next number.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: This is not easy to build. The jump needs a lot of energy in a very short time, and that can make the watch less accurate. That is why many independent watchmakers see the jumping hour as a test of skill. It is a small moment of drama on your wrist.
